content:
Quick answer: If arthritis is making your home hard to manage, start by asking your council (or health and social care trust in Northern Ireland) for a needs assessment, usually by an occupational therapist. They can recommend equipment and adaptations. Bigger changes may be funded by a Disabled Facilities Grant in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, or a mandatory grant under your council's Scheme of Assistance in Scotland.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Disabled Facilities Grants, GOV.UK: Council Tax discounts for disabled people and gov.scot: Funding adaptations to the home. Local rules vary, so always check with your council.

Stairs, a high bath, stiff taps, a step at the front door or a long walk to the bins: when you have arthritis, small features of your home can make a big difference to pain, safety and independence. The good news is that there is more help available than many people realise, from free assessments and equipment to grants for major adaptations and help with housing costs. This guide brings it together in one place, with the differences between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Step 1: Get a needs assessment

The best starting point is usually an assessment by an occupational therapist (OT) or trained assessor. They look at what you find hard at home and recommend equipment, adaptations or other support.

NationWho to contact
England and WalesYour local council's adult social services. GOV.UK says a needs assessment can lead to help such as home care, disability equipment and adaptations to your home.
ScotlandYour local council's social work team. mygov.scot says they will arrange a care needs assessment.
Northern IrelandYour local health and social care trust. Your GP can also refer you.

The assessment is free. Your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team can also refer you to an OT. Before the visit, write down the tasks you struggle with, and when: for example getting in and out of the bath, climbing stairs at the end of the day, or opening the front door during a flare.

Step 2: Small aids and simple changes

Many problems can be solved with equipment or small changes. After an assessment, councils can provide some equipment and minor adaptations; ask what your council offers and whether it charges. Common examples for arthritis include:

  • grab rails by the toilet, bath, shower and front door
  • a second stair rail
  • raised toilet seats, toilet frames and bath boards or seats
  • lever taps, which are easier than twist taps for painful hands
  • a perching stool for the kitchen
  • a key safe or a door entry system, so you do not have to rush to the door
  • chair and bed raisers

Our guide to sheltered housing covers other options if you want extra support close by.

Step 3: Grants for bigger adaptations

England, Wales and Northern Ireland: Disabled Facilities Grants

GOV.UK says you could get a Disabled Facilities Grant (DFG) from your council if you are disabled and need to change your home. Examples include widening doors, installing ramps or grab rails, a stairlift or level-access shower, improving access to your garden, a downstairs bedroom extension, or adapting heating or lighting controls.

NationMaximum grant (GOV.UK, checked 10 October 2026)
EnglandUp to £30,000
WalesUp to £36,000
Northern IrelandUp to £25,000
ScotlandDFGs are not available; see below

Key points from GOV.UK:

  • How much you get usually depends on household income and savings over £6,000. You may need to pay towards the cost.
  • Some councils may give more.
  • Owners and tenants can apply. You must intend to live in the property during the grant period, usually 5 years.
  • A DFG will not affect any benefits you get.
  • Do not start work before the council approves your application, or you might not get any grant.
  • You can apply again for the same property if your condition changes.
  • Foundations, a government-funded organisation, can help you find support to apply.

Our Disabled Facilities Grant guide walks through the application step by step.

Scotland: mandatory grants and the Scheme of Assistance

The Scottish Government's guide for homeowners says your council must give you a grant for changes it judges essential, called a mandatory grant. Everyone gets 80% of the cost covered, and people who get certain benefits get 100%. Some councils top up the 80% depending on income. Each council publishes a Scheme of Assistance setting out what it considers essential and other help it offers. Start with a care needs assessment from your council's social work team.

If you rent

Council and housing association tenants should contact their landlord first, as many landlords have their own adaptations process. Private tenants usually need their landlord's permission for adaptations. If permission is a problem, get advice; your rights under the Equality Act 2010 may help.

Making adaptations work for arthritis

Arthritis is different from many other conditions because symptoms often change from day to day and can get worse over time. When you discuss adaptations, it helps to think about:

  • Your worst days, not just your average day. Describe what happens during a flare, first thing in the morning and in the evening when you are tired.
  • Your hands as well as your legs. Lever handles, push-button controls, easy-grip window catches and a lightweight front door can matter as much as rails and ramps.
  • Future needs. If your arthritis is progressing, ask whether a level-access shower now could save a second set of works later.
  • Heating. Many people find cold makes stiffness worse. GOV.UK lists heating systems suitable for your needs as something a DFG can cover.
  • Safety. If you have had falls, mention them. Rails, better lighting, removing trip hazards and a personal alarm can all reduce risk.

Template: notes for your assessment

  • My condition: [type of arthritis, joints affected, how long I have had it]
  • A typical good day at home: [what I can do]
  • A bad day or flare: [what I cannot do, how often this happens]
  • Hardest rooms and tasks: [e.g. bathroom – cannot get out of bath; stairs – need two hands on the rail]
  • Falls or near misses in the last year: [when, where, what happened]
  • Who helps me now: [name, how often]
  • What I would like to be able to do again: [e.g. have a shower on my own, get into the garden]
  • Home details: [owner or tenant, landlord's name if renting, number of floors]

Step 4: Save money on housing costs

VAT relief on equipment and adaptations

GOV.UK says that if you are disabled or have a long-term illness, you will not be charged VAT on products designed or adapted for your own personal or domestic use, or on their installation, repairs and spare parts. Examples include stairlifts, adjustable beds and building work like ramps, widening doors or installing a lift or toilet. Your condition must qualify: GOV.UK says this includes a physical impairment that affects your ability to carry out everyday activities, or a condition treated as chronic sickness. You usually sign a declaration for the supplier.

Council Tax: Disabled Band Reduction Scheme

GOV.UK says you may qualify if you live in a larger property than you would need if you or another occupant were not disabled, for example because you need an extra bathroom, kitchen or other room, or extra space to use a wheelchair. If you qualify, your bill is reduced to the next lowest band, or by 17% if you are already in Band A. Apply to your council. Northern Ireland uses domestic rates instead of Council Tax, and has its own Disabled Persons Allowance.

Help with rent

  • Universal Credit can include help with housing costs, covering rent and some service charges. Most new claimants of working age claim this instead of Housing Benefit.
  • Housing Benefit still applies for some people, including many over State Pension age.
  • The bedroom rules: GOV.UK says Housing Benefit can be reduced if you live in social housing and have a spare bedroom (14% for one spare bedroom, 25% for two or more). But some people can have their own bedroom, including a couple who cannot share because of a disability or medical condition, and a non-resident overnight carer who sometimes has to stay overnight.
  • Discretionary Housing Payments from your council may help if your benefit does not cover your rent.

Our financial help directory covers other benefits, including PIP, which is not affected by your housing situation.

Step 5: If your home is no longer suitable

Council and housing association homes

GOV.UK says each council has its own rules and uses a points or banding system based on housing need. You are likely to be offered housing first if, for example, you have a medical condition made worse by your current home. Ask your council about its medical priority form, and include evidence from your GP, OT or rheumatology team about how your home affects your arthritis. Some properties are advertised as suitable for disabled people. In Northern Ireland, apply through the Housing Executive; in Scotland and Wales, ask your council.

Sheltered and extra care housing

Sheltered housing offers your own home with a scheme manager or alarm service, and extra care housing adds on-site care. See our guides to sheltered housing and extra care housing.

Buying or moving privately

If you are planning a move, think about how the home will suit you in 10 or 20 years: level access, a downstairs toilet, space for a walk-in shower, parking close to the door and nearby shops and transport. Our retirement planning guide has more on planning ahead.

A home check for arthritis

Walk through your home and tick anything that is difficult. Take this list to your assessment.

  • ☐ Getting in and out of the front door, including steps and the key
  • ☐ Climbing the stairs, especially at the end of the day
  • ☐ Getting on and off the toilet
  • ☐ Getting in and out of the bath or shower
  • ☐ Turning taps, door handles and window catches
  • ☐ Reaching high or low cupboards
  • ☐ Getting up from chairs or out of bed
  • ☐ Carrying shopping, laundry or bins
  • ☐ Keeping the home warm enough
  • ☐ Getting into the garden

Free, independent help

Citizens Advice, Shelter (England), Shelter Scotland, Shelter Cymru, Housing Advice NI, Turn2us, Scope, Disability Rights UK and Age UK offer free information and advice. Many areas also have a home improvement agency that helps older and disabled people arrange adaptations. We are not connected to any of these organisations.

When to get medical help

Speak to your GP if you are having falls, are struggling to look after yourself, or if pain and stiffness are getting worse. They can review your treatment and refer you for physiotherapy or occupational therapy. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with fever. Call 999 if someone has fallen and is badly hurt or cannot get up.

Frequently asked questions

How much is a Disabled Facilities Grant?

On 10 October 2026, GOV.UK said up to £30,000 in England, £36,000 in Wales and £25,000 in Northern Ireland. How much you get usually depends on your income and savings. DFGs are not available in Scotland, which has its own grant system.

Can I get help with adaptations in Scotland?

Yes. Your council must give a mandatory grant for adaptations it judges essential, covering 80% of the cost, or 100% if you get certain benefits. Contact your council's social work team for an assessment.

Will a Disabled Facilities Grant affect my benefits?

No. GOV.UK says a DFG will not affect any benefits you get.

Can I start the work before my grant is approved?

Do not. GOV.UK warns you might not get any grant if you start work before the council approves your application.

Do I pay VAT on a stairlift?

Not if your condition qualifies and the stairlift is for your own personal or domestic use. GOV.UK lists stairlifts as an example.

Can I get a Council Tax reduction because of arthritis?

You may, through the Disabled Band Reduction Scheme, if you need extra space or an extra room because of disability. You may also qualify for income-based Council Tax Reduction from your council.

Can my medical condition help me get a council home?

It can. GOV.UK says councils are likely to offer housing first to people with a medical condition made worse by their current home. Each council has its own rules, so send medical evidence.
